title: Hijab and modesty
hook: Everyone seems to have an opinion about hijab. Here's what Islam actually says, and how real people get there.

screens.text: {women}For many new Muslim women, hijab is the biggest question of all. Today: what the ruling is, how women actually get there, and how people react.{/women}{men}Modesty is part of the deal for every Muslim, men included. Today: what modesty asks of you, and how to treat sisters on their own path.{/men}
**Modesty is for everyone.** The Qur'an tells believers to lower their gaze and guard their private parts [Q 24:30–31].{women} For you, it then adds covering.{/women}
bubbles: Behind it is **haya'**: a sense of dignity and modesty that the Prophet ﷺ called part of faith [Bukhari 9]. It shows in how you look, speak and dress.

screens.prompt: Which of these are part of modesty in Islam?

options.feedback: Yes. It's the first thing the Qur'an asks of every believer [Q 24:30–31].

options.text: Loose clothing that covers what it should
options.feedback: Yes. Modest clothing is part of it for everyone.

options.text: How you speak and carry yourself
options.feedback: Yes. Haya' is inner as well as outer: dignity in words and manners too.
Not quite. It starts with the eyes, words and manners. Clothes are one part, and modesty is everyone's.

variant.default: **The ruling, plainly.** Mainstream scholars of all four schools hold that hijab is required for a Muslim woman past puberty [Q 24:31; Q 33:59].
variant.hanafi: **The ruling, plainly.** Mainstream scholars of all four schools hold that hijab is required for a Muslim woman past puberty [Q 24:31; Q 33:59].

screens.title: A gentle path
screens.intro: The ruling doesn't bend, but the road to it can be gradual. Scholars such as Shaykh Gibril Haddad describe helping a new Muslim toward hijab step by step [Qibla 35720].

steps.text: Many women start with looser clothes
Then a scarf at the masjid

screens.done_text: A step is a path forward, not permission to stop. A sister still working toward it is a Muslim on her way.

screens.prompt: Keisha became Muslim two months ago. She hasn't started wearing hijab yet, but she's learning and working toward it. What's true?

options.text: She's a Muslim with a goal she's working toward; struggling with it isn't rejecting it
options.feedback: Yes. She believes it's required and is taking steps. That's very different from denying the ruling.

options.text: She isn't really Muslim until she covers
options.feedback: Not quite. Hijab is required, but not wearing it yet doesn't cancel her shahada. She's on her way.

options.text: Hijab is optional for new Muslims
options.feedback: Not quite. The ruling applies to her. What's gentle is the pace, not the ruling itself.

screens.situation: Maria starts wearing hijab at her retail job. Her manager says: "It's a little much for customers. Could you leave it off at work?"

options.text: Calmly explain it's part of her religion and ask, in writing, for a religious accommodation. Talk to her mentor, and to CAIR if it's refused
options.feedback: Yes. In the US, employers generally must accommodate religious dress unless it causes real hardship. Calm, written, and with support.

options.text: Take it off at work to avoid trouble, without saying anything
options.feedback: Not quite. She may have more protection than she thinks. Ask first, and talk to her mentor before deciding anything.

options.text: Tell him he's a bigot, in front of customers
options.feedback: Not quite. He may just not know the law. A calm, written request protects her far better.

screens.title: What people might say, and what you could say back

cards.front: A classmate: "Did someone make you wear that?"
cards.back: "Nope, it was my choice. I actually had to work up to it." Short and true.

cards.front: Your mom: "You're hiding the beautiful girl I raised."
cards.back: Hear the love in it. "I'm still me, Mom. This is just how I want to dress now." Give her time.

cards.front: A Muslim at the masjid: "Why aren't you covering yet?"
cards.back: "I'm working on it, in sha Allah." Your path is between you and Allah. You don't owe anyone a timeline.

cards.front: Another Muslim: "Your scarf is wrong. Show less hair."
cards.back: "Thanks, I'll ask my teacher." Then ask a woman you trust. Unasked-for correction isn't the last word.

screens.text: **Brothers, this part is yours.** Modesty for men starts with the eyes: lower your gaze [Q 24:30]. A sudden glance isn't your fault; the Prophet ﷺ told a man to turn his eyes away after one [Muslim 2159].
bubbles: Cover at least navel to knee, in loose clothing. Shorts that end above the knee don't do it.
For sisters: mainstream scholars hold hijab is required for a Muslim woman past puberty [Q 24:31]. It's her worship, at her pace; yours is your own modesty.

screens.situation: At the masjid, Marcus meets a sister who became Muslim recently. She isn't covering yet. A friend nudges him: "Shouldn't someone say something?"

options.text: Keep his own gaze in check, be kind and welcoming like with anyone, and leave her path to her and Allah
options.feedback: Yes. A sister still working toward it is a Muslim on her way. His part is his own modesty.

options.text: Go tell her that hijab is required
options.feedback: Not quite. Don't police sisters' hijab. Their journey isn't your project, and she can ask a woman she trusts.

options.text: Avoid her so it doesn't look like he approves
options.feedback: Not quite. Coldness doesn't help anyone. Be kind, and keep your focus on your own eyes.

screens.text: **Talk to a woman who's been there.** You can ask a female mentor anything about hijab, privately.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Men are told to lower their gaze and guard their private parts; women likewise, and to cover their adornment except what normally shows, drawing their head-coverings over their chests, except before close family listed in the verse [Q 24:30–31]. Women are told to draw their outer garments over themselves [Q 33:59].
- Mainstream scholars hold hijab is obligatory; several advise a gradual approach for converts. Shaykh Gibril Haddad: the ruling stands as prescribed, and a convert may be helped toward it step by step [Qibla 35720]. Al-Qaradawi goes further (tolerating an uncovered head for a time for fear the convert leaves) [IslamOnline]; the app does not adopt that (scholar question Q8). Never present the ruling as optional.
- 'Awrah: men, navel to knee (Hanafis include the knee); women, all except face and hands, with views differing on the feet (Hanafi: feet may show) [Research Notes - Core Essentials §5].
- In Q 24:30–31 men are addressed first (lower the gaze), then women; the lesson teaches it per gender (men's screens 10–12, women's 4–9 and 13), so if asked, say modesty is everyone's and men are addressed first.
- Haya' is part of faith [Bukhari 9]. A sudden glance: turn the eyes away [Muslim 2159].
- Workplace: US Title VII generally requires employers to accommodate religious dress unless it causes undue hardship [EEOC]; CAIR helps with complaints. Day 24 covered accommodation requests.
- Struggling vs denying (Spec §5): a woman not yet wearing hijab who accepts the ruling is a Muslim working on it; denying the ruling is different.

**Likely questions**
- *"Female mentor."* Offer the female mentor or female staff route (rule 12) and the "Ask my imam" queue with a request for a woman to answer, where the masjid has one.
- *"How do I start at work or school?"* Practical: pick a start date, a simple style, a one-line answer for questions, know your accommodation rights; tell the mentor. Don't push a timeline.
- *"My parents are against hijab."* Don't rule. Acknowledge it's hard; the ruling isn't optional, and kindness to parents still applies [Q 31:15]. For a minor, route to a female mentor and the imam (scholar question Q27); for an adult, to the imam. Safety rule 6 first if there are threats.
- *"Does modesty mean I can't wear color or style?"* Modest clothing can be colorful and personal; the standard is coverage, looseness and opacity, not a uniform [Field Guide ch. 10].
- *"Men's modesty day to day?"* Lowering the gaze in person and online, covering navel to knee in loose clothes, respectful speech. If asked about the beard: Day 59 covers it; scholars discuss it; ask the imam.
- *"I took it off. Am I a bad Muslim?"* No shaming. Taking it off is a struggle, not leaving Islam. Encourage gentle return and a female mentor conversation.

**Escalate:** a minor whose parents forbid hijab (scholar question Q27); any request for a personal ruling on removing hijab for safety, a job or a family situation; questions about niqab; any harassment or threat (safety rule 6 and CAIR).

**Don't**
- Don't say hijab is optional, cultural or "only for when you're ready." Don't threaten, shame, or set deadlines.
- Don't let a men's question turn into policing women's dress.
- Don't discuss specific women's bodies or appearance.
madhabNote: Most scholars of the four schools hold that a woman covers everything except her face and hands in front of men outside her close family; some, notably in the Hanbali school, hold the face should be covered too. The Hanafi school also lets the feet show; the Shafi'i and Hanbali schools generally require covering them; Maliki views vary. For men, the Hanafi school counts the knee itself as part of what must be covered; the others cover from the navel to the knee, not including it.
